what_its_for: Fentanyl is a very strong opioid pain medicine used to treat severe, ongoing pain that cannot be controlled by other pain medicines. The patch form is used for around-the-clock pain. The lozenge, film, spray, and tablet forms are used for sudden breakthrough pain in people who are already taking other opioid pain medicines regularly.
how_to_take: How you take fentanyl depends on the form your doctor prescribed: PATCH: Apply the patch to clean, dry, flat skin on your upper arm, chest, back, or side. Press firmly for 30 seconds. Change the patch every 72 hours (3 days) unless told otherwise. Never cut the patch. LOZENGE (Actiq): Place the lozenge in your mouth and move it around your cheek. Do not chew or swallow it whole. Use it over 15 minutes. BUCCAL TABLET (Fentora): Place the tablet between your cheek and gum and let it dissolve. Do not chew, suck, or swallow it. SUBLINGUAL TABLET (Abstral): Place under your tongue and let it dissolve completely. Do not chew or swallow. NASAL SPRAY (Lazanda): Spray into one nostril as directed. SUBLINGUAL SPRAY (Subsys): Spray under your tongue. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions for whichever form you use.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your exact dose based on your pain, your body, and what other pain medicines you take. Doses are very individual. Never change your dose on your own. Never use more than prescribed. For the patch, do not apply more than one patch unless your doctor tells you to. For breakthrough pain forms, wait at least the amount of time your doctor says between doses, and do not use more than the allowed number of doses per day. Fentanyl is much stronger than most other opioids, so even a small extra amount can be life-threatening.
missed_dose: PATCH: If you forget to change your patch on time, apply a new one as soon as you remember and then continue on the new schedule. Do not apply two patches to make up for a missed one unless your doctor says it is okay. BREAKTHROUGH PAIN FORMS: These are used only when you have pain, so there is no regular schedule to miss. Do not take an extra dose just because you feel it is time. If you are unsure, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store all fentanyl products safely away from children and pets — this is extremely important because even used patches or leftover medicine contain enough fentanyl to kill a child or pet. PATCH: Store unused patches at room temperature (59°F to 77°F / 15°C to 25°C) in a secure place. After removing a used patch, fold it sticky-side together and flush it down the toilet immediately. LOZENGES, TABLETS, SPRAYS: Store at room temperature away from heat, moisture, and light. Keep all forms in a locked cabinet if possible. Check for take-back programs in your area to safely dispose of any unused medicine. Never throw fentanyl in the regular trash.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol or use products containing alcohol while using fentanyl — this can cause life-threatening breathing problems. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything requiring alertness until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, and other opioid pain medicines unless your doctor knows about them, as combining them can cause very dangerous breathing problems. Do not expose the patch to heat sources like heating pads, electric blankets, heated waterbeds, hot tubs, saunas, or direct sunlight — heat makes fentanyl release too fast into your body, which can be dangerous. Do not cut, chew, or damage the patch. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as they can increase fentanyl levels in your blood.
when_to_call_doctor: Call 911 or get emergency help RIGHT AWAY if you or someone else has: very slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; blue or purple lips or fingernails; will not wake up or cannot be roused; extreme confusion or disorientation; or a seizure. These are signs of a fentanyl overdose. If available, use naloxone (Narcan) immediately and then call 911. Call your doctor soon if you notice: your patch is not sticking well or has fallen off; you have severe constipation, nausea, or vomiting; you feel extremely dizzy or lightheaded when standing; you develop skin redness, rash, or irritation where the patch is placed; your pain is not being controlled; you feel dependent or are craving higher doses; or you have any new medicines prescribed by another doctor.
when_it_works: PATCH: Fentanyl patches take 12 to 24 hours to start working after you first apply them. Your doctor may give you other pain medicine during this time. It reaches its full effect within 1 to 3 days. When you stop using the patch, fentanyl stays in your body for about 17 hours after removal. BREAKTHROUGH PAIN FORMS: These forms begin to work within 5 to 15 minutes and last for about 30 to 60 minutes, helping to ease sudden pain spikes quickly.
special_populations: CHILDREN: Fentanyl patches should only be used in children 2 years and older who already take opioids regularly. Breakthrough pain forms are generally not recommended for children. Keep all forms completely out of children's reach at all times. ELDERLY (65 and older): Older adults may be more sensitive to fentanyl and have a higher risk of breathing problems, falls, and confusion. Your doctor may start at a lower dose and monitor you more closely. PREGNANCY: Fentanyl can harm an unborn baby and cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in newborns. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. BREASTFEEDING: Fentanyl passes into breast milk and can sedate or harm a nursing baby. Discuss the risks with your doctor before breastfeeding. KIDNEY OR LIVER PROBLEMS: These conditions slow how your body processes fentanyl, which can cause the medicine to build up to dangerous levels. Your doctor will adjust your dose carefully and monitor you more often.
